newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end off, inflation jitters take toll.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end off, inflation jitters take toll.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed down in moderate trade on Tuesday as fears of possible rising inflation took an expensive toll on the market, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended down 12/32 at 94-4/32. Its yield rose to 7.10 percent, up from 7.07 percent at Monday's close.
A strong manufacturing survey by the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond and tepid demand for new 9-3/4-year inflation-indexed Treasury notes also weighed on prices, market experts said.
Analysts said inflation jitters were triggered by a newswire report which included quotes by an official at the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
Some in the market interpreted the report as an indication that consumer inflation data for March, which is scheduled to be released next week, would be higher than expected.

"There was a story on a BLS official who said we could have a high-side reading on the core CPI because of airline fares and clothing prices," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc.

"There was a follow up story that said the official doesn't know what the core CPI is and it should not be viewed as a warning to the market ... But it was out and people are thinking about upside risks for the CPI next Tuesday," he added.
A strong manufacturing index from the Richmond Fed also poured some cold water on the market, traders said.
"We had some elements of the Richmond Fed survey that were not seasonally adjusted, but still the report was pretty strong," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
The survey showed, among other things, the manufacturing new orders index rose to 25 in March from a -1 reading in February.
Weak demand for the Treasury's auction of $8.0 billion in inflation-indexed 9-3/4-year notes also dragged prices down.
The notes were placed at 3.650 percent, with a bid-to-cover ratio of 2.26. "The TIPS auction today was not a strong one ... It was a sloppy auction," a U.S. trader said.
Analysts said the market was also concerned about what the Federal Reserve will do next after it raised the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25.
"The main concern here is still the Fed," said Gary Thayer, senior economist at A.G Edwards and Sons Inc.
"It seems the market is still bracing for another rate increase in May. But the thing to keep in mind is they (the Fed) might not do anything in May," he added.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed unchanged at 5.10 percent. The six-month bill rate rose three basis points to 5.34 percent. The year bill rate was up two points at 5.63 percent.

The two-year note closed down 2/32 at 99-22/32, yielding 6.42 percent. The five-year note traded off 5/32 at 99-15/32 to yield 6.75 percent. The ten-year note closed down 8/32 at 95-15/32, yielding 6.89 percent.
